questions.q: How does availability differ from reliability and recoverability as distinct NFRs?
options: Availability, reliability, and recoverability are all the same measurement under different names
Availability only applies to Government Cloud customers
Availability asks whether the system is up and reachable right now; reliability asks whether it behaves correctly while up; recoverability asks how it returns to a known-good state after a loss event
Reliability and recoverability are both Shield features, while availability is a base-platform feature
questions.explain: These are three genuinely distinct NFRs: a system can be reachable but misbehaving (unreliable), reachable and correct but unable to recover from data loss (not recoverable), or simply unreachable (unavailable) — each needs its own requirement.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about Salesforce publishing a single, universal, numeric uptime percentage as a blanket platform-wide contractual guarantee?
options: Salesforce does not publish one universal numeric uptime guarantee covering the core platform the way some vendors publish a flat SLA; trust.salesforce.com is a transparency/status site, not itself a contractual guarantee, and any specific product's SLA should be verified against its own current signed agreement
Salesforce guarantees exactly 99.999% uptime across the entire platform in every contract
Salesforce has never published any uptime-related information anywhere
The uptime guarantee is always 100%, with no exceptions, for all Salesforce products
questions.explain: trust.salesforce.com publishes real-time and historical status information, which is distinct from a contractually guaranteed percentage with a financial remedy. Some specific products carry their own numeric SLA in their own agreements, but that shouldn't be assumed to apply platform-wide without checking the actual current contract.

questions.q: What does Recovery Time Objective (RTO) actually measure, per this lesson's definition?
options: The maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured in records
The number of backup copies retained at any given time
The percentage of time the system is available over a calendar year
The maximum acceptable time between a disaster and the system being fully functional again — including data, metadata configuration, and active integrations, not just restored rows in a table
questions.explain: RTO is about time-to-functional-recovery, and functional recovery means more than restored data — it means a working org with its metadata configuration and integrations operating again, not merely rows back in a database table.

questions.q: What does Recovery Point Objective (RPO) measure, and what does a tight RPO (e.g., 15 minutes) generally require in terms of design?
options: RPO measures system response time, and a tight RPO requires faster Apex execution
RPO measures the maximum acceptable data loss as a time window, and a tight RPO generally demands continuous or near-real-time replication rather than periodic backups
RPO measures user satisfaction, and a tight RPO requires a better UI
RPO measures governor-limit consumption, and a tight RPO requires asynchronous Apex
questions.explain: RPO defines how much data loss, measured in time, is tolerable in a disaster. A tight RPO like 15 minutes means periodic (e.g., daily or weekly) backups aren't frequent enough — the design needs continuous or near-real-time replication to actually meet that bar.

questions.q: Why does this lesson warn against assuming any single backup mechanism automatically satisfies whatever RTO/RPO number a business names?
options: Because backups are never useful for disaster recovery on Salesforce
Because only third-party tools can ever be used for Salesforce disaster recovery

Because different native and third-party options sit on a spectrum of frequency and restore capability, and the architect's job is matching the actual stated RTO/RPO requirement to a solution that can realistically deliver it
Because Salesforce's native Backup and Restore product guarantees a zero-second RPO by default
questions.explain: Native options range from infrequent exports to more frequent native backup products, and third-party tools can offer still tighter recovery characteristics — the right fit depends on matching the actual RTO/RPO the business has stated, not assuming any available tool automatically covers it.
